paper_title: HotSpot Thermal Floorplan Solver Using Conjugate Gradient to Speed Up

scenario.figure_or_table: Table 1 (also Tables 2-3, MCNC benchmark, ami49 case)
scenario.description: Solver run-time comparison inside the HotSpot simulated-annealing thermal floorplanner. An LU decomposition solver is compared with a conjugate gradient (CG) solver, with and without Jacobi or SSOR preconditioning, on MCNC benchmarks (xerox, hp, ami33, ami49). The paper reports the ami49 case with 49 blocks as the headline result: 1534.41 s for LU versus 134.7 s for SSOR-CG, about an 11.39x speedup. The paper publishes no block coordinates or dimensions and no per-block powers. Block powers were randomly generated by a Perl script with power density between 1e5 and 1e7 W/m2, and the individual values are not published. It reports no temperature observable; the observables are solver CPU run time and speedup ratio.
scenario.architecture: MCNC benchmark block-level floorplans (ami49 with 49 blocks); a 2D HotSpot block thermal resistance model with no stacked-die, interposer or package details published
scenario.workload: Randomly generated block power trace (Perl random function), power density 1e5 to 1e7 W/m2 per block; no real workload
scenario.operating_point: Static temperature evaluation within each simulated-annealing iteration; no published ambient temperature, cooling condition or per-block power values

original_setup.solver: HotSpot thermal-resistance block model (R*T=P), with the default LU decomposition solver compared against a conjugate gradient (CG) solver. CG was run unpreconditioned, with a Jacobi preconditioner, and with an SSOR preconditioner. The incremental CG variant reuses the previous SA iteration's solution as the initial estimate (PDF pages 3-5).
original_setup.optimizer: Simulated Annealing thermal floorplanner in HotSpot (hot floorplan). Cost is lambdaA*Area + lambdaT*Temperature + lambdaW*WireLength (PDF pages 3, 5, 6).
original_setup.controller: None. There is no dynamic thermal management or runtime controller. The solver is switched by a command-line parameter, and the model gives a static temperature evaluation inside each SA iteration (PDF pages 2, 5).
original_setup.benchmark: MCNC benchmark circuits xerox (10 blocks), hp (11), ami33 (33) and ami49 (49), plus GSRC n100, n200 and n300 (Table 4). Selected scenario: MCNC ami49 with 49 blocks, LU 1534.41 s versus SSOR-CG 134.7 s, ratio 11.39 (Tables 1-3, PDF pages 6-7). Block powers were randomly generated by a Perl script with power density 1e5 to 1e7 W/m2 per block, and the individual values are not published. Machine: Ubuntu, Intel Core i5-2300 2.80 GHz, 12 GB memory.

thermal_observable.location: No temperature observable is reported. The paper reports solver CPU run time (s), average per-solve time (s) and speedup ratio. For the selected ami49 scenario the SSOR-CG run time is 134.7 s, the LU run time is 1534.41 s and the ratio is 11.39. The SA cost uses the maximum block temperature, but no value is published.
thermal_observable.aggregation: Not applicable for temperature. Run time is total SA floorplanner CPU time, and the per-solve average is total run time over the number of solver calls.

physical_mismatches.reason: The paper is a numerical linear-solver speed benchmark and reports no temperature, no per-block dimensions or coordinates, no per-block power values, and no ambient or boundary conditions. No complete thermal experiment can be reconstructed from it, so the selected scenario is not steady_2d_relevant.

The optimizer is simulated-annealing floorplanning with a changing placement and a relative-sparse-matrix incremental solver. A fixed-placement thermal evaluation would not reproduce this optimizer or solver behavior.

The model is a 2D HotSpot block thermal resistance model. There is no 3D stacking, interposer or chiplet structure, and no cooling or package specification is published. It is not comparable to chiplet or 2.5D setups.
Block powers come from a random Perl script (power density 1e5 to 1e7 W/m2), so there is no real workload and no transient power trace. There is no controller or reliability analysis.

studio_assumptions: No paper-derived floorplan, power rows or thermal observable exist, so the Studio floorplan is empty.

Any Studio run would be a separate illustrative construction using bundled package and material assumptions. Its generated coordinates and powers would be kept distinct from paper facts, and its temperatures would not be compared numerically to the paper, which reports none.
The Studio solver is not the paper's HotSpot LU or CG solver and runs no simulated-annealing optimizer, so no replication of the paper's run-time results is claimed.
missing_inputs: Per-block x, y, width and height for ami49, or any MCNC case, as used in the paper's runs; the MCNC benchmark data are cited, but no files are pinned.
Per-block powers for the ami49 run. The paper gives only the random density range 1e5 to 1e7 W/m2.
Any temperature observable (maximum or mean block temperature) with its unit and location.
Ambient temperature, package, heat spreader and heat sink, and cooling boundary conditions, and HotSpot configuration files.
Source code, repository, HotSpot configuration or supplementary data. The artifact search found no linked assets and the packet has none pinned, and the paper gives no availability statement or URL.
The Perl power-generation script and random seed.
A power time series. None is published, and the paper's evaluation is static.
